prose.heroLede: I build AI-ready design systems with 1:1 code parity and architect the AI workflows that connect product, design, and engineering. Working alongside Technical Product Managers and developers, I close the traditional handoff: designing the systems, optimising the processes, and contributing directly to PRDs, prototypes, and production code.
prose.cvSummary: I build AI-ready design systems: component libraries with 1:1 parity between Figma and code, plus custom Claude skills and MCP setups that let agents assemble UI from the real system without drift. I write and ship the frontend myself, reviewed and merged by engineering. Under the tooling sits seven years of research practice: user interviews, usability testing, and WCAG 2.1 AA auditing.

background.prose: Before tech, I spent eleven years helping build and grow a strength and nutrition coaching practice. As the owner's close business partner, I took ownership of many of the systems that defined the business. I led a team of coaches, designed the recruitment and onboarding programme, created the assessment framework used across the practice, conducted hundreds of client interviews, and built a data-driven approach to measuring progress and outcomes.
background.statement: It taught me something design school doesn't: people rarely behave the way they say they will. You have to meet them where they are and design not for what they say, not even what they think they want, but for what they truly need at that moment in their journey.

openSource: Tokens are born in the repo, not in Figma. One tokens.json builds the site's CSS variables and a flat JSON that both AI agents and a one-way repo-to-Figma push read — which makes Figma an output of the system rather than its source. Every component ships as a CSS block, a machine-readable spec for agents, and a Storybook story, and the build fails if any of the three is missing, so parity is enforced rather than maintained by hand.
Light and dark come from the same token file: a themed colour carries its dark value beside its light one, and the entire theme is 23 re-aliased tokens with zero per-component rules.

media.caption: One source of truth, four consumers, no manual steps between commit and production.
Figma — variables after the first push

projects.summary: A portfolio built as a product: repo-first design system, compiled copy, an MCP server and a chat assistant answering from one corpus, and a published retrieval evaluation. Open source, no build step in the site.
projects.subtitle: Every claim on this page is inspectable in the same public repository that renders it. If the system were not real, this page could not exist in the shape it does.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A designer's portfolio usually describes process. This one demonstrates it: every button and chip on this page comes from a design system that lives in the same public repository, documents itself for AI agents, and ships automatically. If I claim to build AI-ready systems, the claim should be inspectable. And it goes past styling: every word here is compiled from one authored source, so anything an AI assistant says about me on this site is traceable to a sentence I actually wrote.

sections.heading: The system
sections.text: Repo-first tokens. One JSON file is the only place a colour is born. Zero-dependency scripts generate everything downstream: the CSS custom properties the vanilla pages load, the theme the Next.js app builds on, a machine-readable flat file for AI agents, and the Figma push. Every component is defined once. Its variants, states and token bindings live as data beside the tokens; one pipeline renders them to CSS for the vanilla site, a second generates the typed React components the Next.js site imports. Spec and Storybook story still gate every component: governance as scripts, not a platform.

sections.heading: The pipeline
sections.text: One definition, two renderers. The component definitions compile twice. The first pipeline emits plain CSS classes, and the vanilla pages consume them with two link tags. The second emits a Tailwind theme that exposes every token as a native utility, then generates one typed React component per definition: the variant map derives from the definition's variants, and the utility classes resolve to the theme's tokens. Only behaviour is written by hand: focus, keyboard, ARIA. Appearance cannot drift between the two sites, because neither of them owns it. GitHub → Vercel. Three deployments from one public repo, each its own Vercel project, rebuilt on every push to main: the static site, the Storybook, and the statically exported Next.js front end. Repo → Figma. Tokens flow one way: an AI agent pushes them as Figma Variables following a written, idempotent procedure. Figma is an output, never a source. Repo → AI. CLAUDE.md routes any agent to the system's README and per-component specs; an agent can assemble correct UI from the canonical patterns without seeing the site first.

sections.heading: The words are a pipeline too
sections.text: Every sentence on the site and the CV is authored in one content directory and compiled outward: the page regions, the five case-study pages, a JSON corpus for retrieval, schema.org data, and llms.txt. Copy is moved verbatim, never rewritten by tooling, and a gate byte-compares all ten generated files, so a word of drift fails the build.

sections.heading: Ask the site itself
sections.text: The corpus feeds a retrieval layer: BM25 and embeddings over the shipped chunks, eight tools, and an answer schema whose validation gates reject a claim the corpus cannot support. Two surfaces consume it. An MCP server lets agents install this portfolio as a tool, and the on-page assistant answers with structured blocks resolved against the same corpus. Both draw from what I actually wrote, because nothing else is in the corpus.

sections.heading: Measured, not claimed
sections.text: Retrieval quality is a published number, not a promise. A fixed question set runs against several retrieval arms, the results table and the method live on the evals page, and a committed baseline turns a regression into a failing gate. The eval page's own prose is compiled by the same content pipeline with its figures left as placeholders for the runner to fill, so the page cannot advertise a number the run did not produce.

sections.heading: Receipts
sections.text: 0 accessibility violations across the component library: axe-audited per story, WCAG 2.1 AA contrast decisions documented inside the tokens themselves, and verified in both themes. 83 tokens, 147 values, 23 components. One token carries its light, dark and print values together; each component is enforced as definition + spec + story by the build. Dark mode is 23 tokens and zero component rules. A themed colour carries its dark value beside its light one; the build emits the media query and the pinned-theme override. There is no prefers-color-scheme anywhere in the component CSS: the sharpest test a semantic token layer can be put to. Every boundary crossing is a generated artefact with a schema, never a code import. A gate asserts the dependency direction and pins each legal crossing, and the whole check runs offline, with no API key and no network. A second front end proves it. A Next.js + React + TypeScript app renders the same nine pages from the published package and corpus alone. It exists to make the boundaries falsifiable: the moment it needs another slice's source, the architecture has failed. No build step in the vanilla site. Two link tags consume the system; view-source shows everything.

projects.title: AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows
projects.summary: Green Street's first design system, and the steps that took it from a Figma library into production: a shipped navigation component, an AI prototype pipeline for the TPM team, and a product module rebuilt at 1:1 Figma parity with 100% token coverage.
projects.subtitle: A design system built in Figma, proven in production one green light at a time, now growing into a git-based system that designers, developers and AI agents read from the same source.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.text: Green Street is a leading commercial real estate data and analytics company. I was hired to build their first design system. They had a UI kit and some Figma variables, but the drift between design files and the shipped product was severe; the UX audit found 16 variations of the primary button alone. The system I delivered covers colour, spacing, border radius and typography with a two-level token architecture: primitives, including full Tailwind-style colour ramps, and a semantic layer on top. Text styles are built from the tokens. The base components mirror the shadcn/ui inventory, so every component in the library corresponds to a real coded component, and the set works as a self-sufficient design system.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.text: The system had one problem: it could not reach the codebase. Leadership backed initiatives that bring revenue, and rebuilding the front end around a new component library was not on the roadmap for the next year or more. That left the design system as a Figma artefact. It changed nothing about the development cycle. We still lost hours helping developers get the front end to look similar to the designs, and it was never an exact match. A design system that only exists in Figma is a picture of a design system.

sections.heading: First production code
sections.text: I started with the smallest thing I could ship myself. The header of our platform needed better responsive navigation, so I asked a senior developer to let me build it, explained my front-end experience and how I work with agents, and we agreed on a simple deal: I open a PR, he reviews it. I designed the navigation in Figma, used Claude to learn the codebase's APIs, conventions and style requirements, and wrote the component to match the design exactly, in both pixels and behaviour. The PR was reviewed, approved and merged. It runs in production today.

sections.heading: The TPM prototype pipeline
sections.text: The second step was for the TPM team. They were already using AI tools to mock new features, but stakeholders hesitated to approve mocks that looked nothing like our platform. I built them a component library based on my design system and shadcn, with tokens, layouts, navigation, patterns and design rules, and an agent that assembles feature mocks from those parts. Custom Claude skills handle the maintenance: extracting components from Figma, adding new ones when a feature needs them, keeping tokens in sync. The library never targeted production, so it didn't matter that it wasn't built on our Vue stack. The mocks now look like the product, approvals go through, and TPMs iterate in minutes instead of waiting on design time.

sections.heading: The AI Assistant module
sections.text: Then I was given the redesign of our AI Assistant, a chat module that connects to our own MCP server and answers with text, charts, tables, cards and downloadable content. While designing I read its codebase to learn the limitations, and found something better: the module is a capsule. Its components are written in Vue 3, compiled to Web Components and rendered inside a shadow DOM, so nothing inside it leaks into the rest of the platform. That made it the perfect place to build the way I had been arguing for. The module was still in beta. I took the plan to the project manager, the dev team lead and the global software teams manager, and got a green light to prove it in one PR. The design side came first: a small design system with only the tokens and components this tool needs, every screen built from components, every component built on tokens, and every description and decision documented to be read by agents as much as by people. Then the PR. Every design token became a variable. Text styles became predefined mixins. Every icon joined the library. Every existing component was refactored to remove hardcoded values; some needed simple replacement, some needed behavioural work. I also built a styleguide that renders the real components from the code, so I could verify every gap and spacing in the inspector myself. The work ran as a phased plan written by Claude and executed by different agents, with me reviewing between phases. Figma MCP supplied the tokens and designs, but on complex components its output drifts from the design, so every component was checked by hand against the old hardcoded values. After some sleepless nights and readjustments, all 35 components were on the token architecture, written in SCSS variables and mixins, at 1:1 parity with Figma and 100% token coverage, with functionality fully preserved and automated tests in the PR. For QA I added a small agent that reads the repo and drafts acceptance criteria and manual test suggestions per component. The PR was accepted. The team kept building on the tokens and base components, and the module now has a design system its developers and their agents can both read.

sections.heading: In progress: the git-based system
sections.text: That case earned a bigger mandate: not just the design system, but the workflow around it. What I'm building now, prototyped but not yet approved, is a contract-first, git-based system. Tokens and components live in the repository as the master copy, with design decisions and their rationales recorded beside them. Every change is a pull request, verified in CI. Each build generates a machine-readable contract, and every surface is produced from that contract: the component package, the styleguide, an MCP endpoint for agents, and the Figma library, which is pushed automatically. Designers keep designing in Figma; the repository holds the truth. Because everything flows one way, two copies of a fact cannot disagree.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.text: The responsive navigation is merged and live in production. The AI Assistant module runs on tokens: 35 components, 1:1 Figma parity, 100% coverage, and the team keeps building on them. TPM prototypes now look like the product, and approvals go through. A contract-first, git-based design system exists as a working prototype, awaiting approval. The proof that this architecture works is the page you are reading. A personal version of the same system builds this portfolio: tokens, components and every word of copy live in one public repository, CI verifies every generated artefact, and pipelines emit the site, the Storybook, the Figma variables and an MCP server that answers from the same source. It is smaller than the Green Street plan because its only user is me, not because it does less.

projects.title: UX & Accessibility Audits
projects.summary: UX and WCAG 2.1 AA audits of two product surfaces: an editorial platform and a data-dense analytics platform. 200+ issue instances covering accessibility, consistency, visual hierarchy, and UI patterns, ordered into a remediation roadmap.
projects.subtitle: End-to-end UX and accessibility audits of an editorial platform and a data-dense analytics platform: WCAG 2.1 AA compliance plus consistency, hierarchy, layout, and pattern choice, delivered as severity-rated, annotated remediation roadmaps.

sections.heading: Why it matters here
sections.text: Green Street's users are professional analysts, investors, and brokers making high-stakes financial decisions. Many work across multiple screens for hours; some use assistive technologies. For a data company, an unlabelled filter or a contrast failure is a credibility gap.

sections.heading: Green Street News: the editorial platform
sections.text: Colour contrast. Systematic review against WCAG 2.1 AA thresholds across article bodies, bylines, timestamps, and navigation. Semantic structure. Heading hierarchy that reads correctly in a screen reader, not only on the page. Keyboard navigation. Focus traps, missing indicators, mouse-only elements. Labelling. Icon-only buttons, ambiguous "read more" links, unlabelled form controls.

sections.heading: Analytics & Research Platform: data-dense
sections.text: Data tables. Header scope, captions, sortable column accessibility, nested headers. Charts. Text alternatives, colour-only encoding, keyboard-accessible data views. Filters and faceted search. Keyboard operability, focus management, live region announcements. Dynamic content. Explicit focus management for async loading, panels, and modals. Full AA sweep. A criterion-by-criterion review of all 50 success criteria that apply at Level AA.

sections.heading: The UX track
sections.text: Accessibility was one lens. The other was UX and UI quality across both products: consistency of components and styles, colour and typography hierarchy, layout, and the choice of UI patterns. This is where the drift showed at its clearest: the audit catalogued 16 variations of the primary button alone, and the most inconsistent patterns later became the first components standardised in the design system.

sections.heading: Deliverables
sections.text: Issue instances catalogued across the two surfaces. Every finding carries a severity rating (Critical / Major / Minor), an annotated screenshot, a recommended fix, and an estimate of engineering effort; accessibility findings also cite the WCAG criterion they fail. Each finding is mapped to the platform workflow it affects, so engineering unblocks the most-used analytical paths first. The output is a prioritised remediation roadmap, not a list of complaints.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.text: Both products have a clear, actionable roadmap to WCAG 2.1 AA compliance. Cross-product observations shaped component prioritisation in the AI-ready design system: the most inconsistent patterns became the first to be standardised. A repeatable audit methodology for every new product surface as the platform grows. Once the design system lands, accessibility stops being an audit finding and becomes a build-time guarantee: every component passes its accessibility checks before it can ship, enforced by CI gates.

projects.title: Cleaning Service Marketplace

metrics.label: reduction in front page bounce rate

projects.summary: Multi-year, research-led UX on Bulgaria's leading cleaning marketplace. Front page, flows, onboarding, loyalty: bounce rate down 40%, retention up.
projects.subtitle: A research-led, multi-year UX engagement on Bulgaria's leading cleaning services marketplace, with every design change grounded in evidence rather than assumption.

sections.heading: The brief
sections.text: Domestina runs as a marketplace: cleaning companies and independent professionals compete for clients on reputation, reviews, and pricing. That makes three user types with three definitions of success: clients booking a service and deciding who to trust, service providers competing on reputation, and housemaids needing a low-friction onboarding path. The challenge was to serve all three without making any of them feel second-class.

sections.heading: Research
sections.text: Competitor analysis showed Domestina had no direct comprehensive competitor in the Bulgarian market; it had to define its own UX standards rather than borrow from a category leader. Personas built from user interviews, provider phone interviews, support tickets, Google Analytics, and Hotjar surfaced the critical insight: clients were anxious about inviting a stranger into their home. Trust signals, concretely reviews, profile completeness, response time, and verified badges, were the primary conversion driver, and they had to be immediately visible rather than buried.

sections.heading: What I changed
sections.text: Front page redesign. Hotjar recordings showed users arriving, scrolling briefly, and leaving. The page was doing three jobs at once: marketing the platform, recruiting providers, and helping clients book, all fighting for prominence. I restructured the hierarchy around the primary client action, moved trust signals above the fold, and gave provider recruitment its own entry point. Domestina Club. A virtual loyalty card for returning clients, designed into the existing flows so the mechanics reinforced booking behaviour without adding friction to the primary conversion path. Provider workshops. Working sessions revealed that providers cared about their ranking but had little idea what affected it. Design changes made performance feedback clear and actionable, and a better-performing provider pool improved outcomes for clients in turn. Housemaid registration. The form was long, the value proposition unclear, and nothing showed momentum. I rebuilt it with progressive disclosure: named stages, visible progress, and non-essential fields deferred until after registration.

sections.heading: Measured outcomes
sections.text: 40% reduction in front page bounce rate from a focused hierarchy redesign, not a full rebuild. Marked increase in completed housemaid registrations. Improved retention following the Domestina Club launch. Stronger provider performance after workshop-driven design changes. Not a single project: a continuous improvement methodology applied to a live, growing marketplace over multiple years.

projects.title: Municipal Mobile App
projects.summary: Civic app serving tourists and older residents at once. White-label token system. Live on the App Store and Google Play.
projects.subtitle: End-to-end design of a cross-platform civic app serving two opposing audiences, tourists and older residents, live on the App Store and Google Play.

sections.heading: The challenge
sections.text: Malko Tarnovo is a small municipality in southeast Bulgaria, known for its nature reserves, historical sites, and an older resident population. Its app had to serve two audiences with almost opposing needs. Tourists are explorers: they want visual richness, maps, and discovery flows. Local residents, many of them older, need municipal services: waste schedules, announcements, contacts, with large touch targets, minimal cognitive load, and zero ambiguity.

sections.heading: Information architecture
sections.text: Research started with how similar municipal apps handle the tourist and resident split, stakeholder interviews about the most-used services, and a map of the municipality's existing communications. The resulting information architecture separates the two content domains at the top level while sharing one navigation pattern and one component library. Users self-select into a context, tourism or municipal services, and the app never forces them to declare which they are. The structure was validated with card sorting and flow walkthroughs before any visual design.

sections.heading: The dual colour logic
sections.text: Green encodes everything tourism: nature reserves, trails, gastronomy, connecting to the Strandzha region's identity. Blue encodes everything administrative, carrying the institutional calm of government services. The colour is a wayfinding system, not decoration. A user glancing at a card knows whether it is a tourist recommendation or a municipal service before reading a word. For older users, colour becomes a cognitive shortcut. And because the logic lives in semantic tokens rather than hardcoded values, the entire system can be recoloured for another municipality without touching a component.

sections.heading: White-label design system
sections.text: Semantic colour tokens. Primary, secondary, surface, border, and status colours as variables. Swap the green and blue for any municipality's brand and the change cascades through the whole system. Spacing and rounding tokens. One spacing scale for every padding, margin, and gap, and radius values as variables, so the app's character can shift from rounded and friendly to sharp and institutional with a single change. Typography system. Comfortaa, tokenised scale, friendly enough for tourism and readable enough for official communications. Icon system. The municipal logo redesigned on a 64×80 grid aligned to the layout grid, coherent from app icon to in-app header.

sections.heading: Accessibility by default
sections.text: Touch targets at or above 44×44px throughout, the WCAG AAA target size, to accommodate older users. WCAG 2.1 AA contrast across both colour contexts. Hierarchy through size, weight, and spacing, never colour alone. Progressive disclosure for dense municipal content: summary cards that expand, not long scrolling pages.

sections.heading: Components, not compositions
sections.text: Every screen was built from components rather than one-off compositions, so a component change propagated across all screens and the developer handoff was a component map instead of static images. A fully interactive Figma prototype covered the primary flows for both audiences and served stakeholder review, developer reference, and a final usability walkthrough before handoff.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.text: Launched on iOS and Android, publicly available on both stores. The white-label system is a reusable product: any Bulgarian municipality can deploy it with brand-token changes alone. The dual colour logic became a reference model for designing civic services for mixed-age audiences.

projects.title: Spetema
projects.summary: A 200+ product coffee catalogue serving households and businesses from one site. Split navigation, a preparation-method finder, eight sub-brands on a shared attribute model. Bilingual, live.
projects.subtitle: A 200+ product coffee catalogue reconciling B2C e-commerce and B2B corporate needs on a single coherent site, with a bold visual system and purposeful motion. Bilingual, live.

sections.heading: The challenge
sections.text: Spetema's audience is genuinely dual-natured. Consumers browse discovery-led, where visual appeal converts. Business and horeca buyers, café owners and procurement teams, move task-led, where clarity converts. Optimise purely for one and you frustrate the other.

sections.heading: Information architecture
sections.text: The existing site had grown reactively for years: 200+ products spread across overlapping categories, the B2B offer with no clear entry point, corporate information buried. I split the top level into two tracks, a home track and a business track, so both audiences orient within seconds instead of filtering past each other's content. Underneath, a preparation-method finder layers over the category taxonomy. Category trees are organised the way a business classifies coffee; a lot of people shop by the machine sitting on their counter. The finder lets them enter that way without the taxonomy being rebuilt around it. Eight sub-brands are structured on a shared attribute model, so product information is authored once and surfaced everywhere it's needed: consumer detail pages, B2B catalogue, homepage features, without duplication.

sections.heading: Visual system
sections.text: Strong typographic hierarchy. Large, confident headlines with clear reading order. Product-first imagery. UI frames the photography rather than competing with it. Modular components. The same card renders a consumer product, a business service, or an article. Purposeful motion. Every animation reviewed against one question: does this help the user understand what's interactive? Decoration was removed.

sections.heading: Validation
sections.text: A/B variants for navigation wording, hero layout (product-first versus brand-story-first), B2B entry prominence, and grid density, evaluated with stakeholders and lightweight user testing. Winners were the approaches that worked for both audiences, not just one.

sections.heading: Status
sections.text: Live and bilingual. Handoff used annotated Figma components with motion specs: everything the team needed to implement the system faithfully, without back-and-forth.

components.a11y: A real <button> with a permanent aria-label; the visible label folds away on scroll but the accessible name never does. Drawer wiring (aria-expanded/aria-controls) rides on the same attributes the bar's Ask uses.
Use <a> to navigate and <button> to act; the global :focus-visible ring is never suppressed.
Titles are <h3> inside a section headed by <h2> — the heading order is the contract.
Headings are <h3> under the page's <h1>; the list marker is drawn with ::before, so it is decoration rather than content a screen reader reads out.
Thread is role=log aria-live=polite; the composer keeps focus while busy (aria-disabled + readOnly, never the disabled attribute).
Display-only <span>. Anything that responds to a click is a Button instead.
role=dialog aria-modal=true labelled by its title; the focus trap, Escape and focus restore are mandatory, and the opener carries aria-expanded.
Role is <h3> under the section <h2>; bullet glyphs are ::before so the list is still announced as a list.
All three parts are required — a number with no label is unreadable; the counter degrades to plain text without JS or with reduced motion.
The only inverse surface on the page; its label token is rated against that surface in both themes.
External links carry target=_blank rel=noopener and a trailing arrow; labels name the destination, never 'click here'.
Every real needs meaningful alt text describing the content, never 'screenshot'.
role=dialog aria-modal on the sheet; focus trapped while open, Escape closes, focus returns to the Menu segment. The trigger's aria-expanded is the announcement and the lit state in one fact.
<nav aria-label="Primary">; the status dot is aria-hidden and hover states hold AA contrast.
Real <dl>/<dt>/<dd> semantics, each pair wrapped in a <div> for the grid.
Project rows are <button>s; .idx__go is aria-hidden because the whole row is the target.
Always an <h2>; the note is hidden under 640px, so it may never carry essential information.
Rails and strips are decoration: js/automata.js sets aria-hidden on every one, its canvas carries none of the page's meaning, and content never goes in them.
Real <ol>/<li>; the ordinal is content inside the item, not a CSS counter a screen reader would skip.
A framed number inside prose — it adds no semantics, so the sentence around it has to still read correctly.
Pure decoration: it carries aria-hidden, holds no content and is never focusable or announced — its only job is to be the height nobody's words are using.
A real <button> with three states, so no aria-pressed; the aria-label carries the current state and what activating does.
Display levels are uppercased by CSS, so source text stays normal case and is announced as words rather than letters.

html: Plain lexical search won on ranking, and the structured arm lost. BM25 reaches {{evals:bm25.hit3}} hit@3 and {{evals:bm25.mrr}} MRR; navigating by name reaches {{evals:tools-only.hit3}} and {{evals:tools-only.mrr}}. The design being evaluated here expected the opposite, and the number is reported the way it came out. The reason is visible in the failures: a name match fires on whichever entity happens to share a word with the question, and on questions phrased the way people actually phrase them — “what user research methods does he use?” — no entity is named at all. The corpus is small, single-author and lexically consistent, which is precisely the condition under which BM25 is strong.

Knowing when to say nothing is where they separate, and it is not close. BM25 abstains on {{evals:bm25.abstained}} of {{evals:abstention.total}} unanswerable questions. It returns a confident ranked list for “did he ever work at Google?” — the word appears eight times in the corpus, in Google Analytics, Google Play and Google AI Studio, none of them an employer — and for “what are his salary expectations?”, and for “does he speak Japanese?”. The tools arm abstains on {{evals:tools-only.abstained}} of {{evals:abstention.total}}, because no entity was named. That is not a tuning artefact; it is the difference between matching words and resolving identifiers.

Fusing the two rankings made both worse. Tools-first with BM25 appended scores {{evals:hybrid.hit3}} hit@3 — below BM25 alone — and abstains on nothing, because the fallback always fires. It inherits the weaker ranking and the weaker judgement. That result killed the originally proposed shape, which is the most useful thing this table did.

What the failure suggested instead. Stop fusing rankings and split responsibilities: let the name match decide whether the corpus covers the question, and let BM25 decide what comes back once it does. That arm — tools-gated — holds {{evals:tools-gated.hit3}} hit@3 and {{evals:tools-gated.separability}} separability, tied for best in the table, while raising the abstention rate to {{evals:tools-gated.abstain}}. Roughly seven points of ranking traded for the entire ability to say “not on file”. It is labelled post-hoc everywhere it appears, because it was written after seeing the first three arms on this same question set; it is a hypothesis this run suggests, not a result this run establishes, and it needs questions written after it to become one.

Two holes in the corpus, found by the eval rather than by a reviewer. Location, availability and contact details live in content.json as structured fields and appear in no chunk, so “where is he based?” cannot be answered by any search over prose — the only chunk containing the word “Sofia” is the education line, about Sofia University, and BM25 duly returns something else entirely. Separately, the 2007–2009 quality assurance role has no bullet points, so the content build produced no chunk for it at all: the role is in the index and invisible to search, and every arm scores zero on it. Both are why the tool layer reads structured fields directly instead of searching for them.

One question no arm could answer, and it is the case for embeddings. “How far has he run?” shares no term with “42 km. Marathon finisher.” — lexical search returns nothing at all. That is the exact shape of question a semantic retriever exists for. The embeddings arm has since been run: it answers this question and wins every retrieval class, at {{evals:embeddings.hit3}} hit@3 against BM25's {{evals:bm25.hit3}}. The argument became a measurement.

The point the corpus statistics make on their own. The complete table of contents — every project id, title, client, tag and one-line summary, every role and span — is a few thousand characters. It fits in the system prompt. A retriever exists to solve “I cannot enumerate what is in here”; when the whole index fits in the prompt, that problem does not exist, and provisioning a stateful, billed service to solve it anyway is a decision about a résumé rather than about a corpus. That argument survives this table. The claim that structured lookup also ranks better did not.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Multi-year, research-led UX on Bulgaria's leading cleaning marketplace. Front page, flows, onboarding, loyalty: bounce rate down 40%, retention up.

chunks.heading: Subtitle
chunks.text: A research-led, multi-year UX engagement on Bulgaria's leading cleaning services marketplace, with every design change grounded in evidence rather than assumption.

chunks.heading: The brief
chunks.text: Domestina runs as a marketplace: cleaning companies and independent professionals compete for clients on reputation, reviews, and pricing. That makes three user types with three definitions of success: clients booking a service and deciding who to trust, service providers competing on reputation, and housemaids needing a low-friction onboarding path. The challenge was to serve all three without making any of them feel second-class.

chunks.heading: Research
chunks.text: Competitor analysis showed Domestina had no direct comprehensive competitor in the Bulgarian market; it had to define its own UX standards rather than borrow from a category leader. Personas built from user interviews, provider phone interviews, support tickets, Google Analytics, and Hotjar surfaced the critical insight: clients were anxious about inviting a stranger into their home. Trust signals, concretely reviews, profile completeness, response time, and verified badges, were the primary conversion driver, and they had to be immediately visible rather than buried.

chunks.heading: What I changed
chunks.text: Front page redesign. Hotjar recordings showed users arriving, scrolling briefly, and leaving. The page was doing three jobs at once: marketing the platform, recruiting providers, and helping clients book, all fighting for prominence. I restructured the hierarchy around the primary client action, moved trust signals above the fold, and gave provider recruitment its own entry point. Domestina Club. A virtual loyalty card for returning clients, designed into the existing flows so the mechanics reinforced booking behaviour without adding friction to the primary conversion path. Provider workshops. Working sessions revealed that providers cared about their ranking but had little idea what affected it. Design changes made performance feedback clear and actionable, and a better-performing provider pool improved outcomes for clients in turn. Housemaid registration. The form was long, the value proposition unclear, and nothing showed momentum. I rebuilt it with progressive disclosure: named stages, visible progress, and non-essential fields deferred until after registration.

chunks.heading: Measured outcomes
chunks.text: 40% reduction in front page bounce rate from a focused hierarchy redesign, not a full rebuild. Marked increase in completed housemaid registrations. Improved retention following the Domestina Club launch. Stronger provider performance after workshop-driven design changes. Not a single project: a continuous improvement methodology applied to a live, growing marketplace over multiple years.

chunks.heading: Subtitle
chunks.text: End-to-end UX and accessibility audits of an editorial platform and a data-dense analytics platform: WCAG 2.1 AA compliance plus consistency, hierarchy, layout, and pattern choice, delivered as severity-rated, annotated remediation roadmaps.

chunks.heading: Why it matters here
chunks.text: Green Street's users are professional analysts, investors, and brokers making high-stakes financial decisions. Many work across multiple screens for hours; some use assistive technologies. For a data company, an unlabelled filter or a contrast failure is a credibility gap.

chunks.heading: Green Street News: the editorial platform
chunks.text: Colour contrast. Systematic review against WCAG 2.1 AA thresholds across article bodies, bylines, timestamps, and navigation. Semantic structure. Heading hierarchy that reads correctly in a screen reader, not only on the page. Keyboard navigation. Focus traps, missing indicators, mouse-only elements. Labelling. Icon-only buttons, ambiguous "read more" links, unlabelled form controls.

chunks.heading: Analytics & Research Platform: data-dense
chunks.text: Data tables. Header scope, captions, sortable column accessibility, nested headers. Charts. Text alternatives, colour-only encoding, keyboard-accessible data views. Filters and faceted search. Keyboard operability, focus management, live region announcements. Dynamic content. Explicit focus management for async loading, panels, and modals. Full AA sweep. A criterion-by-criterion review of all 50 success criteria that apply at Level AA.

chunks.heading: The UX track
chunks.text: Accessibility was one lens. The other was UX and UI quality across both products: consistency of components and styles, colour and typography hierarchy, layout, and the choice of UI patterns. This is where the drift showed at its clearest: the audit catalogued 16 variations of the primary button alone, and the most inconsistent patterns later became the first components standardised in the design system.

chunks.heading: Deliverables
chunks.text: Issue instances catalogued across the two surfaces. Every finding carries a severity rating (Critical / Major / Minor), an annotated screenshot, a recommended fix, and an estimate of engineering effort; accessibility findings also cite the WCAG criterion they fail. Each finding is mapped to the platform workflow it affects, so engineering unblocks the most-used analytical paths first. The output is a prioritised remediation roadmap, not a list of complaints.

chunks.heading: Outcomes
chunks.text: Both products have a clear, actionable roadmap to WCAG 2.1 AA compliance. Cross-product observations shaped component prioritisation in the AI-ready design system: the most inconsistent patterns became the first to be standardised. A repeatable audit methodology for every new product surface as the platform grows. Once the design system lands, accessibility stops being an audit finding and becomes a build-time guarantee: every component passes its accessibility checks before it can ship, enforced by CI gates.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Green Street's first design system, and the steps that took it from a Figma library into production: a shipped navigation component, an AI prototype pipeline for the TPM team, and a product module rebuilt at 1:1 Figma parity with 100% token coverage.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: Subtitle
chunks.text: A design system built in Figma, proven in production one green light at a time, now growing into a git-based system that designers, developers and AI agents read from the same source.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: The brief
chunks.text: Green Street is a leading commercial real estate data and analytics company. I was hired to build their first design system. They had a UI kit and some Figma variables, but the drift between design files and the shipped product was severe; the UX audit found 16 variations of the primary button alone. The system I delivered covers colour, spacing, border radius and typography with a two-level token architecture: primitives, including full Tailwind-style colour ramps, and a semantic layer on top. Text styles are built from the tokens. The base components mirror the shadcn/ui inventory, so every component in the library corresponds to a real coded component, and the set works as a self-sufficient design system.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: The problem
chunks.text: The system had one problem: it could not reach the codebase. Leadership backed initiatives that bring revenue, and rebuilding the front end around a new component library was not on the roadmap for the next year or more. That left the design system as a Figma artefact. It changed nothing about the development cycle. We still lost hours helping developers get the front end to look similar to the designs, and it was never an exact match. A design system that only exists in Figma is a picture of a design system.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: First production code
chunks.text: I started with the smallest thing I could ship myself. The header of our platform needed better responsive navigation, so I asked a senior developer to let me build it, explained my front-end experience and how I work with agents, and we agreed on a simple deal: I open a PR, he reviews it. I designed the navigation in Figma, used Claude to learn the codebase's APIs, conventions and style requirements, and wrote the component to match the design exactly, in both pixels and behaviour. The PR was reviewed, approved and merged. It runs in production today.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: The TPM prototype pipeline
chunks.text: The second step was for the TPM team. They were already using AI tools to mock new features, but stakeholders hesitated to approve mocks that looked nothing like our platform. I built them a component library based on my design system and shadcn, with tokens, layouts, navigation, patterns and design rules, and an agent that assembles feature mocks from those parts. Custom Claude skills handle the maintenance: extracting components from Figma, adding new ones when a feature needs them, keeping tokens in sync. The library never targeted production, so it didn't matter that it wasn't built on our Vue stack. The mocks now look like the product, approvals go through, and TPMs iterate in minutes instead of waiting on design time.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: The AI Assistant module
chunks.text: Then I was given the redesign of our AI Assistant, a chat module that connects to our own MCP server and answers with text, charts, tables, cards and downloadable content. While designing I read its codebase to learn the limitations, and found something better: the module is a capsule. Its components are written in Vue 3, compiled to Web Components and rendered inside a shadow DOM, so nothing inside it leaks into the rest of the platform. That made it the perfect place to build the way I had been arguing for. The module was still in beta. I took the plan to the project manager, the dev team lead and the global software teams manager, and got a green light to prove it in one PR. The design side came first: a small design system with only the tokens and components this tool needs, every screen built from components, every component built on tokens, and every description and decision documented to be read by agents as much as by people. Then the PR. Every design token became a variable. Text styles became predefined mixins. Every icon joined the library. Every existing component was refactored to remove hardcoded values; some needed simple replacement, some needed behavioural work. I also built a styleguide that renders the real components from the code, so I could verify every gap and spacing in the inspector myself. The work ran as a phased plan written by Claude and executed by different agents, with me reviewing between phases. Figma MCP supplied the tokens and designs, but on complex components its output drifts from the design, so every component was checked by hand against the old hardcoded values. After some sleepless nights and readjustments, all 35 components were on the token architecture, written in SCSS variables and mixins, at 1:1 parity with Figma and 100% token coverage, with functionality fully preserved and automated tests in the PR. For QA I added a small agent that reads the repo and drafts acceptance criteria and manual test suggestions per component. The PR was accepted. The team kept building on the tokens and base components, and the module now has a design system its developers and their agents can both read.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: In progress: the git-based system
chunks.text: That case earned a bigger mandate: not just the design system, but the workflow around it. What I'm building now, prototyped but not yet approved, is a contract-first, git-based system. Tokens and components live in the repository as the master copy, with design decisions and their rationales recorded beside them. Every change is a pull request, verified in CI. Each build generates a machine-readable contract, and every surface is produced from that contract: the component package, the styleguide, an MCP endpoint for agents, and the Figma library, which is pushed automatically. Designers keep designing in Figma; the repository holds the truth. Because everything flows one way, two copies of a fact cannot disagree.

cite.label: Green Street — AI-ready design systems and Agentic workflows

chunks.heading: Outcomes
chunks.text: The responsive navigation is merged and live in production. The AI Assistant module runs on tokens: 35 components, 1:1 Figma parity, 100% coverage, and the team keeps building on them. TPM prototypes now look like the product, and approvals go through. A contract-first, git-based design system exists as a working prototype, awaiting approval. The proof that this architecture works is the page you are reading. A personal version of the same system builds this portfolio: tokens, components and every word of copy live in one public repository, CI verifies every generated artefact, and pipelines emit the site, the Storybook, the Figma variables and an MCP server that answers from the same source. It is smaller than the Green Street plan because its only user is me, not because it does less.

cite.label: Municipality of Malko Tarnovo — Municipal Mobile App

chunks.heading: The challenge
chunks.text: Malko Tarnovo is a small municipality in southeast Bulgaria, known for its nature reserves, historical sites, and an older resident population. Its app had to serve two audiences with almost opposing needs. Tourists are explorers: they want visual richness, maps, and discovery flows. Local residents, many of them older, need municipal services: waste schedules, announcements, contacts, with large touch targets, minimal cognitive load, and zero ambiguity.

cite.label: Municipality of Malko Tarnovo — Municipal Mobile App

chunks.heading: Information architecture
chunks.text: Research started with how similar municipal apps handle the tourist and resident split, stakeholder interviews about the most-used services, and a map of the municipality's existing communications. The resulting information architecture separates the two content domains at the top level while sharing one navigation pattern and one component library. Users self-select into a context, tourism or municipal services, and the app never forces them to declare which they are. The structure was validated with card sorting and flow walkthroughs before any visual design.

chunks.heading: The dual colour logic
chunks.text: Green encodes everything tourism: nature reserves, trails, gastronomy, connecting to the Strandzha region's identity. A user glancing at a card knows whether it is a tourist recommendation or a municipal service before reading a word. For older users, colour becomes a cognitive shortcut. chunks.heading: White-label design system
chunks.text: Semantic colour tokens. Primary, secondary, surface, border, and status colours as variables. One spacing scale for every padding, margin, and gap, and radius values as variables, so the app's character can shift from rounded and friendly to sharp and institutional with a single change. Typography system. Comfortaa, tokenised scale, friendly enough for tourism and readable enough for official communications. Icon system. The municipal logo redesigned on a 64×80 grid aligned to the layout grid, coherent from app icon to in-app header.

chunks.heading: The idea
chunks.text: A designer's portfolio usually describes process. This one demonstrates it: every button and chip on this page comes from a design system that lives in the same public repository, documents itself for AI agents, and ships automatically. If I claim to build AI-ready systems, the claim should be inspectable. cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: The system
chunks.text: Repo-first tokens. One JSON file is the only place a colour is born. Zero-dependency scripts generate everything downstream: the CSS custom properties the vanilla pages load, the theme the Next.js app builds on, a machine-readable flat file for AI agents, and the Figma push. Every component is defined once. Its variants, states and token bindings live as data beside the tokens; one pipeline renders them to CSS for the vanilla site, a second generates the typed React components the Next.js site imports. Spec and Storybook story still gate every component: governance as scripts, not a platform.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: The pipeline
chunks.text: One definition, two renderers. The component definitions compile twice. The first pipeline emits plain CSS classes, and the vanilla pages consume them with two link tags. The second emits a Tailwind theme that exposes every token as a native utility, then generates one typed React component per definition: the variant map derives from the definition's variants, and the utility classes resolve to the theme's tokens. Only behaviour is written by hand: focus, keyboard, ARIA. Appearance cannot drift between the two sites, because neither of them owns it. GitHub → Vercel. Three deployments from one public repo, each its own Vercel project, rebuilt on every push to main: the static site, the Storybook, and the statically exported Next.js front end. Repo → Figma. Tokens flow one way: an AI agent pushes them as Figma Variables following a written, idempotent procedure. Figma is an output, never a source. Repo → AI. CLAUDE.md routes any agent to the system's README and per-component specs; an agent can assemble correct UI from the canonical patterns without seeing the site first.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: The words are a pipeline too
chunks.text: Every sentence on the site and the CV is authored in one content directory and compiled outward: the page regions, the five case-study pages, a JSON corpus for retrieval, schema.org data, and llms.txt. Copy is moved verbatim, never rewritten by tooling, and a gate byte-compares all ten generated files, so a word of drift fails the build.

chunks.heading: Ask the site itself
chunks.text: The corpus feeds a retrieval layer: BM25 and embeddings over the shipped chunks, eight tools, and an answer schema whose validation gates reject a claim the corpus cannot support. Two surfaces consume it. An MCP server lets agents install this portfolio as a tool, and the on-page assistant answers with structured blocks resolved against the same corpus. Both draw from what I actually wrote, because nothing else is in the corpus.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: Measured, not claimed
chunks.text: Retrieval quality is a published number, not a promise. A fixed question set runs against several retrieval arms, the results table and the method live on the evals page, and a committed baseline turns a regression into a failing gate. The eval page's own prose is compiled by the same content pipeline with its figures left as placeholders for the runner to fill, so the page cannot advertise a number the run did not produce.

cite.label: This site — Portfolio as a Product

chunks.heading: Receipts
chunks.text: 0 accessibility violations across the component library: axe-audited per story, WCAG 2.1 AA contrast decisions documented inside the tokens themselves, and verified in both themes. tokens, values, components. One token carries its light, dark and print values together; each component is enforced as definition + spec + story by the build. Dark mode is tokens and zero component rules. A themed colour carries its dark value beside its light one; the build emits the media query and the pinned-theme override. There is no prefers-color-scheme anywhere in the component CSS: the sharpest test a semantic token layer can be put to. Every boundary crossing is a generated artefact with a schema, never a code import. A gate asserts the dependency direction and pins each legal crossing, and the whole check runs offline, with no API key and no network. A second front end proves it. A Next.js + React + TypeScript app renders the same nine pages from the published package and corpus alone. It exists to make the boundaries falsifiable: the moment it needs another slice's source, the architecture has failed. No build step in the vanilla site. Two link tags consume the system; view-source shows everything.

chunks.heading: The challenge
chunks.text: Spetema's audience is genuinely dual-natured. Consumers browse discovery-led, where visual appeal converts. Business and horeca buyers, café owners and procurement teams, move task-led, where clarity converts. Optimise purely for one and you frustrate the other.

chunks.heading: Information architecture
chunks.text: The existing site had grown reactively for years: 200+ products spread across overlapping categories, the B2B offer with no clear entry point, corporate information buried. I split the top level into two tracks, a home track and a business track, so both audiences orient within seconds instead of filtering past each other's content. Underneath, a preparation-method finder layers over the category taxonomy. Category trees are organised the way a business classifies coffee; a lot of people shop by the machine sitting on their counter. The finder lets them enter that way without the taxonomy being rebuilt around it. Eight sub-brands are structured on a shared attribute model, so product information is authored once and surfaced everywhere it's needed: consumer detail pages, B2B catalogue, homepage features, without duplication.

chunks.text: Strong typographic hierarchy. Large, confident headlines with clear reading order. Product-first imagery. UI frames the photography rather than competing with it. Modular components.
